article_text:
In Barcelona, ​​Galeria RociSantaCruz presents the Mariaelena Roqué exhibition UnaDonaUna · AutoRetratsRetratats until November 21, 2026.

Mariaelena Roqué is an artist who is difficult to classify and, for that very reason, a singular figure in Catalan contemporary art.

Historically, her career has been linked to the Compañía Carles Santos (Santos-Roqué), which she founded with the musician, an iconic avant-garde group of the 1980s and 1990s. Their actions provocatively blended music, dance, performing arts and visual poetry.

Yet this affiliation does not begin to define the breadth of her individual practice, developed through experimentation and freedom of media.

Mariaelena Roqué’s work is built at the intersection of the visual arts, sculpture, costume-characters, stage action and audiovisual work. It is not bound to any one discipline, but appropriates different languages.

In her costume-character-sculptures, the body and its psyche become, simultaneously, the support and the subject of the work. The human silhouette, in its projection into space, expands, conceals itself or transforms until it acquires a hybrid condition between body, object and sculpture.

From the position of a woman and an artist, her practice brings a critical eye to the construction of identity and gender roles. Radically committed to women’s rights, she uses the female body as a space of expression, evolution and resistance.

This freedom to move between media allows her work to be understood as essentially interdisciplinary, in which matter, body, image, movement and space relate to and transform one another.

RocioSantaCruz’s proposal thus offers an approach to the work of Mariaelena Roqué, drawing on the richness and complexity of a practice that overflows the boundaries between genres and explores, through multiple media, the relationships between body and identity.

In doing so, it makes room for a silenced voice, reaffirming Roqué as an indispensable figure of feminist and contemporary art.

Mariaelena Roqué : UnaDonaUna · AutoRetratsRetratats until November 21, 2026 Galeria RociSantaCruz Gran Vía de les Corts Catalanes 627 08010 Barcelona www.rociosantacruz.com

article_text:
For Morocco’s national pavilion at the 61st International Art Exhibition – La Biennale di Venezia, artist Amina Agueznay and curator Meriem Berrada present Asǝṭṭa , a monumental installation conceived for the Artiglierie in the Arsenale. Taking its title from an Amazigh word for ritual weaving, the project grew from a collaboration between Agueznay and Berrada that began with Noise and developed through a 2018 weaving workshop in Assilah.

Wool, raffia and embroidered threads cascade from towering steel structures, their intricate surfaces bearing the imprint of generations of Moroccan artisans. Suspended between sculpture and architecture, these richly textured forms create an immersive landscape of shifting patterns and passageways, shaped by the contributions of 166 craftspeople from across the country. This is Asǝṭṭa , the monumental work by artist Amina Agueznay, curated by Meriem Berrada, presented as Morocco’s first official national pavilion at the 61st International Art Exhibition – La Biennale di Venezia. Situated in the Arsenale, the pavilion marks a significant moment in Morocco’s institutional representation at the Biennale, placing the ingenuity and artistry of its craftspeople at the centre of an ambitious contemporary vision.

Taking its title from an Amazigh term associated with ritual weaving, Asǝṭṭa draws on traditions passed between generations, particularly among women whose skills have sustained cultural identities and connections to place. These practices preserve histories rarely captured in written archives, finding expression through material, gesture and collective memory. The work takes its architectural inspiration from the âatba , the threshold in Moroccan vernacular architecture, inviting visitors to experience the passage between the familiar and the unknown, private and public, tradition and experimentation.

The project builds on Agueznay and Berrada’s longstanding collaboration, which deepened through a workshop in Assilah in 2018. Their engagement with artisans has developed into a sustained exploration of the relationships between makers, materials and the communities in which their practices are rooted. Rather than treating craftsmanship as a static inheritance, Asǝṭṭa reveals its capacity for reinvention, challenging conventional distinctions between art and craft, individual authorship and collective creation. As Morocco establishes its official national presence at the Venice Biennale, the work offers a vision of cultural identity shaped by exchange, adaptation and the often-unacknowledged labour through which traditions remain alive.

For ART AFRICA , Suzette Bell-Roberts speaks with Amina Agueznay and Meriem Berrada about their collaboration, the artisans behind Asǝṭṭa , and the significance of presenting Morocco’s living cultural traditions within the international framework of the Venice Biennale. Amina Agueznay, Asǝṭṭa , installation view. Courtesy of the Ministry of Youth, Culture and Communication of the Kingdom of Morocco © Matteo Losurdo

How has that history shaped Asǝṭṭa , and how have your roles as artist and curator influenced one another’s thinking?

Amina Agueznay: Meriem and I have worked together for a long time. Her curatorial focus lies at the intersection of contemporary art and craft, so our interests align. One project led to another, like beads on a string. From Curriculum Vitae ( What is Forgotten and What Remains , Musée de l’Immigration, Paris, 2021) to Fieldworks (solo exhibition, Loft Art Gallery, Marrakech, 2025), a red thread runs from each installation to the next, culminating in Asetta in Venice.

Meriem Berrada: Amina has influenced the way I curate, allowing the work to unfold at its own pace. I grew up in Fez, with a sensitivity to architecture and craftsmanship, but working with her taught me to look beyond a piece’s beauty or technical precision and focus on the thinking behind it. When we worked on bringing Noise to the MACAAL in 2018, she insisted we spend a day in Asilah, where it was made. The work could not be understood separately from those encounters. That has stayed with me. With Asǝtta, the curatorial work began long before there was a finished installation to organise. It meant accompanying a work as it emerged. Our dialogue moves constantly between what Amina discovers through matter, how she deconstructs signs and symbols and what I bring through research and conceptual development. I would say the spatial development of the exhibition is where we meet. Venice gave that ongoing conversation another scale. Amina Agueznay, Asǝṭṭa, 2026, installation view. Courtesy of the Moroccan Ministry of Youth, Culture and Communication ©️ Ayoub El Bardii

Asǝṭṭa refers to ritual weaving, but the project approaches weaving as more than a material process — as a means through which knowledge, relationships and memory are constructed. How did this understanding of weaving develop between you?

AA: This question is similar to the first , so I will explain my process here. My entry point to weaving was through architecture and design, then two decades of fieldwork interacting with artisans across different regions. This process involves building trust, experimenting with materials, and collecting stories.

MB: For me, it became clearer through watching how knowledge circulates the loom. Everything happens before the first thread is stretched: preparing and washing the wool, spending time together, exchanging stories. Then comes the concentration of weaving itself, and the rituals that mark its beginning and completion. In several Moroccan cultures, woven work is understood through the cycle of a living being. That changes how one thinks about an object and the relationships it carries.

This understanding also shaped the exhibition. We wanted to give space to the time of making, to the pauses and transitions that allow a relationship to develop. The threshold became important here: entering a workshop, being welcomed, learning to look. The visitor enters another part of that process. Amina Agueznay, Asǝṭṭa, 2026, detail. Courtesy of the Moroccan Ministry of Youth, Culture and Communication ©️ Ayoub El Bardii

The work emerges through relationships with spinners, embroiderers, basket-makers, jewellers, apprentices and master artisans. When many people hold and transmit knowledge, how do you think about authorship, and whose presence remains visible in the finished work?

AA: What is visible and what is experienced are two different things – there is an intangible presence that permeates the work. Everybody who contributed to this project is present, in the work, in the catalogue, in the signage. But the true presence is intangible: the gesture, the trust between artist and artisan, curator and exhibition designers, the atelier chief and head of production, the multisensory experience of raw wool, light, and metal. This human gesture and interaction with matter creates an energy of love and integrity.

MB: What can I add to that? Perhaps one story that stays with me. Yamna, a master weaver from the Khemisset region, produces a weave so tight that it cannot be embroidered. Amina responded to this particular quality by rethinking its place within the installation. To me, this says a great deal about how the work takes shape collectively: one person’s way of working the thread can redirect the composition. Yamna’s presence is there, in the density of her weave and in the form it helped bring into being. Amina Agueznay, Asǝṭṭa, 2026, detail. Courtesy of the Moroccan Ministry of Youth, Culture and Communication ©️ Ayoub El Bardii

Language around craft and heritage can easily become nostalgic, particularly through terms such as “ancestral” and “traditional”. How do you resist fixing these practices in the past and recognise them as changing, inventive and contemporary forms of knowledge?

AA: I don’t see these terms as nostalgic. Without tradition, one cannot innovate. My artistic approach is to explore materiality and test hypotheses. This question rests on a common misconception: that working in textiles, for example, is somehow craft rather than painting or sculpture.

MB: I share Amina’s reluctance to treat these words as inherently nostalgic. What concerns me is the assumption that a practice becomes contemporary only once an artist takes an interest in it. The people who carry these skills are already experimenting, adjusting to materials, teaching and making decisions in the present. Working with Amina has made me question the hierarchies through which we recognise those decisions. Why should thought be readily attributed to one medium and reduced to dexterity in another? In Asǝṭṭa, inherited techniques shape how the work thinks and takes form.

The âatba , or threshold, sits at the conceptual centre of Asǝṭṭa—between inside and outside, private and public, sacred and profane. Why did the threshold become so important to the work, and does it offer a way of thinking about how knowledge moves between different worlds?

AA: Threshold is the architectural concept of transition – negative space or in-between space. This is what interests me. When you enter the artisan’s space, they welcome you into their practice, which is an intimate experience. That is what Asetta offers the viewer: an invitation into a private space where I tell stories. The curatorial intention is to graft a second skin onto the existing environment of the Arsenale in which multiple installations succeed one another. The skin is composed of a series of vertical bands that detach from the walls, creating spaces of passage where stories take place.

MB: The âatba is foundational to Asǝṭṭa . It also runs through Amina’s practice, particularly her relationship to space, which owes much to her first life as an architect. She pays attention to how we enter a place, how we move through it, what it reveals or holds back. In Asǝṭṭa, the threshold acquires depth; it becomes a space we can inhabit, and this shapes our encounter with the work.

For me, this resonates with Abdelkébir Khatibi’s resistance to fixed ideas of identity, his way of thinking different inheritances together. Knowledge moves through people, places and encounters, and changes along the way. The threshold gives us a way to consider those transformations while remaining attentive to the particular histories each person brings. Amina Agueznay, Asǝṭṭa, 2026, installation view. Courtesy of the Moroccan Ministry of Youth, Culture and Communication ©️ Ayoub El Bardii

Asǝṭṭa brings practices and relationships rooted in particular Moroccan places into one of contemporary art’s most international settings. How much needs to be translated for a Venice audience, and what do you deliberately allow to remain culturally specific or not immediately accessible?

AA: There is no intention to translate the work to the viewer – there is only the invitation to enter and create their own experience. A poetry of human interaction unfolds, evoking moments of curiosity. Interstices, for example, is a series of silver elements inserted between the bricks of a former passageway. These delicately crafted pieces are placed there to reactivate the closure, inviting a curious observer to examine it further.

Viewers might experience the entire installation or each work, with sunlight filtering through woven bands, or pause in their journey. One of the works, L’guelssa, is a place to rest, to contemplate, where the viewer becomes performer. The artist activates the vertical space of Interstices, while the viewer activates the horizontal space of L’guelssa.

MB: There is a distinction between offering context and explaining everything in advance. We can give visitors names, places and an account of how the work was made, while allowing their first encounter to remain sensory. The light, the weight of wool, the distance between two modules or the possibility of sitting down can already establish a relationship.

We wanted to retain words such as âatba and Asǝṭṭa because no English equivalent carries all their associations. Those associations can open gradually. Visitors arrive with their own memories of textiles, domestic spaces or protective objects; these may produce connections we could not anticipate.

The work is also specifically in conversation with Venice. The histories explored around the shriâa and the Venetian Rosetta suggest how an object can travel and take on new meanings. That possibility of transformation interests me more than making everything immediately familiar. Curator Meriem Berrada and Artist Amina Agueznay, Aseṭṭa . Created by artist Amina Agueznay. Courtesy of the Ministry of Youth, Culture and Communication of the Kingdom of Morocco © Matteo Losurdo

A national pavilion places an artwork within the framework of representing a country. Morocco contains multiple languages, regions, histories and cultural traditions. How do you work within that framework while resisting the expectation that a single project can stand for “Morocco”?

AA: This seems to be a misinterpretation of representation – whose expectation do you refer to? The intention is not to depict Morocco, but to offer an artistic vision that deserves the distinction of representing Morocco. Asetta is not about exalting a single aspect of Morocco, nor should it be. I’m the first artist to represent Morocco in Venice, but I won’t be the last.

MB: I approach that responsibility with precision in the proposal. We submitted a project grounded in Amina’s practice, in relationships developed over many years, in an encounter with this particular site and in the specific resonance with the “minor keys” conceptual framework. That is the basis on which I can speak as a curator.

Morocco’s plurality is already present in the work, through the different regions, materials, techniques, and individual trajectories that meet within it. We did not need to assign each of them a representative role. Their differences shape the forms themselves. I hope this pavilion makes room for a demanding artistic proposition to be encountered on its own terms, and opens possibilities for what follows. A first pavilion’s responsibility includes leaving that space open. Amina Agueznay, Asǝṭṭa, 2026, detail. Courtesy of the Moroccan Ministry of Youth, Culture and Communication ©️ Ayoub El Bardii

In Minor Keys asks us to attend to quieter narratives and ways of knowing, while Asǝṭṭa takes monumental form. How do monumentality and the “minor” coexist in the installation, and can something monumental still direct attention to gestures, labour and knowledge that have historically remained less visible?

AA: Asǝṭṭa is indeed monumental in scale and scope. In fact, it was originally conceived as a monumental loom within the exhibition space – in which woven bands are stretched to create membrane and thresholds.

For me, the essence of “minor” lies in the musical reference. Works in major key resonate as affirmed, or resolved, whereas works in minor key are more introspective. This distinction speaks to me. With Asetta, we created a large-scale environment in which gesture and craft create intervals and rhythms—a way of experiencing the world.

MB: When I read Koyo Kouoh’s concept, I immediately thought of Amina. Her work develops a force through restraint, through attention to gestures and materials one might otherwise pass by. That affinity was central to our decision to propose the project.

For me, the question is where the monumentality takes you. In Asǝṭṭa , a view of the whole leads you towards a knot, a piece of beadwork, a change in the density of a weave. Moving closer changes the scale again. The intervals matter as much as the accumulation: they allow the eye and the body to pause.

The installation gives these gestures a spatial presence large enough to inhabit, while asking for an intimate kind of attention. I hear the resonance with “In Minor Keys” in that invitation to spend time with what is usually less visible, and to recognise the people and knowledge that sustain it.

"ALF：我将我的实践描述为跨学科的、以研究为驱动的以及对场地有应答性的。我的工作横跨版画、艺术家书、素描、摄影、录像、动画和装置，但我并不认为这些媒介是彼此孤立的。我对当一种媒介的结构和过程开始为一个媒介提供信息时会发生什么很感兴趣。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "版画和素描依然是基础，因为它们与过程、迭代和物质参与有着深厚的联系。我不认为版画仅仅是复制图像的手段，而是组织信息、时间和感知的一种方式。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "贯穿我作品的一条主要线索是我所谓的“体验式警觉”（experiential watchfulness）：对特定场地的持续观察、记录、研究和参与。我可能会花时间在风景中漫步、拍摄照片或制作素描、研究档案材料、考查其环境历史，并思考这些不同形式的知识是如何交织的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种研究常常引导我走向那些风景承载着复杂历史的地方，尤其是那些受工业化、开采、迁徙、环境退化和修复影响的场地。我对即使在实体证据开始消失时这些历史如何依然存在很感兴趣。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "艺术家书变得尤为重要，因为它为我提供了一种使这些层次转化为体验的方式。一本书具有节奏和时间跨度。观众必须翻页、展开结构、在序列中穿行，或者以身体去操纵这个物体。意义正是通过这种互动产生的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这与我对手头当代图像环境的更广泛兴趣息息相关。我们每天都会接触到大量的图像，而大多数图像都被设计成几乎瞬间就被消费完毕。我的作品探讨的是当我们构建抗拒这种速度的图像时会发生什么。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "因此，我将版画和书籍艺术视为历时性的图像系统。它们为持续的观看、反思和身体参与创造了条件。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "实践中的环境维度也变得越来越重要。我尝试过回收的摄影材料、掺入本地采集植物材料的手工纸、植物染料、回收纤维以及其他对场地有应答性的材料。对我而言，材料的选择并非与作品的概念关切分离开来。创作的伦理与过程本身就成了研究的一部分。", "translated": true}, {"type": "text": "ALF：我将自己创作实践的下一阶段视为进一步推进这些想法的契机。我特别有兴趣继续探讨艺术家书、扩展版画媒介、摄影与环境研究之间的关系。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "作品已日益介于单幅版画、书籍与装置之间，而我想继续探索当这些形式重叠时会发生什么。我也对超越作为艺术品或图像容器的手工书感兴趣。我将其视为一种研究方法：一种通过排版、装订、材料和读者互动，将风景转化为认知、时间和具身经验的结构。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "由于最近搬到了缅因州，我开始思考这项研究如何通过对缅因州海岸和南部风景的持续投入来发展。我希望以塑造我在俄亥俄州东北部作品的那种同样的体验式警觉来接触这一新地区，花时间关注特定地点，并让这些地方的环境、文化和历史复杂性通过观察和研究逐渐显现出来。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "地理位置的转变也带来了新的问题。缅因州海岸和南部在土地与水、工业与环境、乡村与城市空间、旅游业与当地社区之间包含着非常不同的关系。我希望让这些差异来塑造作品，而不是简单地将现有的方法论搬到一个新的地点。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我和埃里克·沃特科特（Erik Waterkotte）共同开展的策展工作 Genius "我也在通过写作和会议发言继续深化这项研究。我最近的学术成果考察了作为研究方法的手工书，而我即将进行的会议工作则探讨了版画、书籍艺术以及通过时间、身体存在和具身互动展开的扩展媒介形式。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "刚刚开始担任贝茨学院（Bates College）艺术与视觉文化助理教授的我，对教学、研究和工作室实践能够相互启发感到十分兴奋。我希望在继续发展自己作品的同时，为学生们创造机会去探索手工书、独立出版、另类摄影工艺以及版画的扩展创作方法。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": article_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "Arron Levi Foster: Almost, Everything"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://lenscratch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/©Arron-Foster_Du-und-ich_A.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Lenscratch"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "©Arron Levi Foster, Du und ich A, Cyanotype on post consumer waste"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I’ve been acquainted with Arron Levi Foster’s work for a few years now. I first came across it through the exhibition landscapes: peculiar interpretations , exhibited through Midwest Nice Art , an art collective I founded with my husband, Tim Rickett, and has since exhibited with us numerous times. His primary focus, landscapes, is one of the oldest subject matters in the art world, but the images are anything but typical. Foster’s attention to material is admirable, being able to turn everyday scenes into a profoundly unique experience, incorporating screenprinting, cyanotypes, with handmade paper, fabic, and installation. I’m always very drawn to artists who are willing to experiment and work prolifically, and Foster does both. I highly recommend following along with his work, you will be inspired!", "links": [{"text": "Arron Levi Foster’s", "url": "https://arronfosterstudio.com/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://lenscratch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/©Arron-Foster_Du-und-ich_B.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Lenscratch"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "©Arron Levi Foster, Du und ich B, Cyanotype on post consumer waste"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Arron Foster is a printmaker, interdisciplinary artist, and educator whose work explores landscape, memory, and the shifting boundaries between personal and public space. He holds an MFA in Printmaking and Book Arts from University of Georgia and a BFA in Printmaking and Art Education from East Carolina University. He currently serves as an Assistant Professor of Art and Visual Culture at Bates College."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Working across printmaking, artists’ books, drawing, video, animation, and installation, Foster employs research-driven and site-responsive methodologies that position print as both index and archive. His projects frequently emerge through sustained engagement with specific environments, translating physical terrain, memory, and lived experience into layered visual forms that examine the relationships between place, history, and human intervention."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "His work has been exhibited nationally and internationally, including solo exhibitions at George Fox University, Waterloo Arts, Dayton Society of the Arts, Akron Soul Train Gallery, and Hiram University, as well as participation in the 5th Global Print Exhibition in Portugal and others"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Follow Arron on Instagram: @arron_foster_studio"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://lenscratch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/©Arron-Foster_Du-und-ich_C.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Lenscratch"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "©Arron Levi Foster, Du und ich C, Cyanotype on post consumer waste"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Almost, Everything"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "My practice operates at the intersection of material process, sustained observation, and environmental history, positioning printmaking, photography, and artists’ books as durational image systems. Rather than offering instantaneous visual consumption, my work explores what happens when an artwork invites viewers to slow down, engage physically, and encounter an image as an active, sensory event."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "At the core of this work is experiential watchfulness, a methodology grounded in deep, sustained research into landscapes shaped by extraction, industrial activity, contamination, and remediation. The Mogadore Road series investigates these complex environmental histories across brownfield and Superfund sites in Northeast Ohio, such as the former RB&W industrial fastener plant in Kent. Here, industrial residue intersects with ongoing ecological repair and human memory. Working across handmade paper, recycled fibers, silkscreen, and tactile structures like flag books and tunnel books, the series embraces visual ambiguity. These landscapes hold a quiet tension between physical beauty and environmental degradation, allowing physical materials and spatial sequences to participate directly in the conceptual investigation of place."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Almost, Everything forms a key project within the larger Mogadore Road series, extending this inquiry into process, material limitation, and temporal presence. Developed using a supply of expired photographic paper and simple pinhole cameras, the project documents sites along the Cuyahoga River basin. The inherent qualities of the pinhole process require extended presence at each location, transforming the act of photographing into a prolonged engagement with the site. Formatted as an elongated accordion book, Almost, Everything translates these pinhole images into a sequential, tactile object where the viewer physically unfolds the landscape over time."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Across the Mogadore Road series and Almost, Everything, an image is never a static or unmediated record of a place; it is a material translation. Through physical interaction, such as turning a page, shifting a sight line, or unfolding a sequence, the viewer enters a space where duration, process, and touch become vital ways of knowing."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://lenscratch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/©Arron-Foster_Du-und-ich_D.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Lenscratch"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "©Arron Levi Foster, Du und ich D, Cyanotype on post consumer waste"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Epiphany Knedler: How did your project come about?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Arron Levi Foster: This project developed out of a longer investigation into how we experience and remember place. My background is rooted in printmaking and drawing, and early in my practice I became interested in the fact that printmaking is inherently process-based. An image is built through layers, repetition, translation, and accumulation. I began to wonder whether those qualities could be used not only to construct an image, but to structure how an image is experienced."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "That question eventually led me beyond the singular print toward sequential structures, artist’s books, and installation. I became increasingly interested in what happens when an image cannot be consumed instantaneously, but instead unfolds through time. Pages turn, structures expand, images accumulate, and the viewer has to physically participate in the work."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "At the same time, my research became increasingly focused on particular landscapes and the histories embedded within them. Since 2022, I have been working extensively with Superfund and brownfield sites across Northeast Ohio, including locations in Kent, Mogadore, Deerfield, Akron, and Canton. These are places shaped by extraction, industry, environmental degradation, and remediation, but they are also places where people live, remember, and construct identities."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The project grew out of that intersection between material process, sustained observation, and environmental history. More recently, this thinking came together through my pinhole photography and artist’s book Almost, Everything . While working in my home darkroom, I acquired a large quantity of expired photographic paper. Rather than seeing that material as obsolete, I began thinking about reuse, limitation, and chance as productive parts of the process. I used simple pinhole cameras to photograph sites along the Cuyahoga River, where the varied exposures required me to remain with each location for an extended period."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Those photographs eventually became an elongated accordion book. The project reinforced a question that continues to shape my practice: What happens when an image asks us to slow down?"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://lenscratch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/©Arron-Foster_Sown-with-salt_Mogadore-Road_C.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Lenscratch"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "©Arron Levi Foster, Sown with salt, Mogadore Rd. (series), Lumen Print, Pigment Print, Handmade Paper, Screenprint"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "EK: Is there a specific image that is your favorite or particularly meaningful to this series?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "ALF: I am particularly drawn to the landscape imagery in Sown with Salt . What interests me is the tension between the visual experience of the landscape and the complicated environmental history of the places where the images were made."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The project centers on the Mogadore Road brownfield site in Kent, Ohio, the former location of the RB&W industrial fastener plant. The area has a long history of industrial activity and contamination, followed by an ongoing process of remediation. The surrounding landscape can be visually compelling, but that beauty exists alongside a much more complicated history."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "That ambiguity is important to me. I don’t want the image to tell the viewer simply that this is a beautiful landscape or that this is a damaged landscape. Both things can be true at the same time. The image becomes a way of entering a larger conversation about memory, environmental change, and the ways we construct meaning around place."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "That becomes even more apparent when the imagery enters the book. In Sown with Salt , I use structures such as tunnel books and flag books to layer and repeat images. A tunnel book compresses multiple visual layers into a single sight line, while a flag book creates movement and repetition as it is handled. The image therefore isn’t fixed. It changes depending on how the viewer physically encounters it."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "For me, the photograph or print is only one part of the experience. The structure of the book, the paper, the printing process, and the viewer’s physical movement all contribute to the meaning of the image."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://lenscratch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/©Arron-Foster_Du-und-ich_E.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Lenscratch"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "©Arron Levi Foster, Du und ich E, Cyanotype on post consumer waste"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "EK: Can you tell us about your artistic practice?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "ALF: I describe my practice as interdisciplinary, research-driven, and site-responsive. I work across printmaking, artists’ books, drawing, photography, video, animation, and installation, but I don’t think of those mediums as isolated from one another. I am interested in what happens when the structures and processes of one medium begin to inform another."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Printmaking and drawing remain foundational because they are deeply connected to process, iteration, and material engagement. I think of print not simply as a means of reproducing an image, but as a way of organizing information, time, and perception."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A major thread running through my work is what I call experiential watchfulness: sustained acts of observing, documenting, researching, and engaging a particular site. I might spend time walking a landscape, making photographs or drawings, studying archival materials, researching its environmental history, and considering how those different forms of knowledge intersect."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "That research often leads me toward places where the landscape carries complicated histories, particularly sites affected by industrialization, extraction, migration, environmental degradation, and remediation. I am interested in how those histories remain present even when the physical evidence begins to disappear."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The artist’s book has become particularly important because it gives me a way to make those layers experiential. A book has rhythm and duration. The viewer has to turn a page, unfold a structure, move through a sequence, or physically manipulate the object. Meaning is produced through that interaction."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This connects to my larger interest in the contemporary image environment. Arron Levi Foster: Almost, Everything

©Arron Levi Foster, Du und ich A, Cyanotype on post consumer waste

I’ve been acquainted with Arron Levi Foster’s work for a few years now. I first came across it through the exhibition landscapes: peculiar interpretations , exhibited through Midwest Nice Art , an art collective I founded with my husband, Tim Rickett, and has since exhibited with us numerous times. His primary focus, landscapes, is one of the oldest subject matters in the art world, but the images are anything but typical. Foster’s attention to material is admirable, being able to turn everyday scenes into a profoundly unique experience, incorporating screenprinting, cyanotypes, with handmade paper, fabic, and installation. I’m always very drawn to artists who are willing to experiment and work prolifically, and Foster does both. I highly recommend following along with his work, you will be inspired!

©Arron Levi Foster, Du und ich B, Cyanotype on post consumer waste

Arron Foster is a printmaker, interdisciplinary artist, and educator whose work explores landscape, memory, and the shifting boundaries between personal and public space. He holds an MFA in Printmaking and Book Arts from University of Georgia and a BFA in Printmaking and Art Education from East Carolina University. He currently serves as an Assistant Professor of Art and Visual Culture at Bates College.

Working across printmaking, artists’ books, drawing, video, animation, and installation, Foster employs research-driven and site-responsive methodologies that position print as both index and archive. His projects frequently emerge through sustained engagement with specific environments, translating physical terrain, memory, and lived experience into layered visual forms that examine the relationships between place, history, and human intervention.

His work has been exhibited nationally and internationally, including solo exhibitions at George Fox University, Waterloo Arts, Dayton Society of the Arts, Akron Soul Train Gallery, and Hiram University, as well as participation in the 5th Global Print Exhibition in Portugal and others

Follow Arron on Instagram: @arron_foster_studio

©Arron Levi Foster, Du und ich C, Cyanotype on post consumer waste

Almost, Everything

My practice operates at the intersection of material process, sustained observation, and environmental history, positioning printmaking, photography, and artists’ books as durational image systems. Rather than offering instantaneous visual consumption, my work explores what happens when an artwork invites viewers to slow down, engage physically, and encounter an image as an active, sensory event.

At the core of this work is experiential watchfulness, a methodology grounded in deep, sustained research into landscapes shaped by extraction, industrial activity, contamination, and remediation. The Mogadore Road series investigates these complex environmental histories across brownfield and Superfund sites in Northeast Ohio, such as the former RB&W industrial fastener plant in Kent. Here, industrial residue intersects with ongoing ecological repair and human memory. Working across handmade paper, recycled fibers, silkscreen, and tactile structures like flag books and tunnel books, the series embraces visual ambiguity. These landscapes hold a quiet tension between physical beauty and environmental degradation, allowing physical materials and spatial sequences to participate directly in the conceptual investigation of place.

Almost, Everything forms a key project within the larger Mogadore Road series, extending this inquiry into process, material limitation, and temporal presence. Developed using a supply of expired photographic paper and simple pinhole cameras, the project documents sites along the Cuyahoga River basin. The inherent qualities of the pinhole process require extended presence at each location, transforming the act of photographing into a prolonged engagement with the site. Formatted as an elongated accordion book, Almost, Everything translates these pinhole images into a sequential, tactile object where the viewer physically unfolds the landscape over time.

Across the Mogadore Road series and Almost, Everything, an image is never a static or unmediated record of a place; it is a material translation. Through physical interaction, such as turning a page, shifting a sight line, or unfolding a sequence, the viewer enters a space where duration, process, and touch become vital ways of knowing.

©Arron Levi Foster, Du und ich D, Cyanotype on post consumer waste

Epiphany Knedler: How did your project come about?

Arron Levi Foster: This project developed out of a longer investigation into how we experience and remember place. My background is rooted in printmaking and drawing, and early in my practice I became interested in the fact that printmaking is inherently process-based. An image is built through layers, repetition, translation, and accumulation. I began to wonder whether those qualities could be used not only to construct an image, but to structure how an image is experienced.

That question eventually led me beyond the singular print toward sequential structures, artist’s books, and installation. I became increasingly interested in what happens when an image cannot be consumed instantaneously, but instead unfolds through time. Pages turn, structures expand, images accumulate, and the viewer has to physically participate in the work.

At the same time, my research became increasingly focused on particular landscapes and the histories embedded within them. Since 2022, I have been working extensively with Superfund and brownfield sites across Northeast Ohio, including locations in Kent, Mogadore, Deerfield, Akron, and Canton. These are places shaped by extraction, industry, environmental degradation, and remediation, but they are also places where people live, remember, and construct identities.

The project grew out of that intersection between material process, sustained observation, and environmental history. More recently, this thinking came together through my pinhole photography and artist’s book Almost, Everything . While working in my home darkroom, I acquired a large quantity of expired photographic paper. Rather than seeing that material as obsolete, I began thinking about reuse, limitation, and chance as productive parts of the process. I used simple pinhole cameras to photograph sites along the Cuyahoga River, where the varied exposures required me to remain with each location for an extended period.

Those photographs eventually became an elongated accordion book. The project reinforced a question that continues to shape my practice: What happens when an image asks us to slow down?

©Arron Levi Foster, Sown with salt, Mogadore Rd. (series), Lumen Print, Pigment Print, Handmade Paper, Screenprint

EK: Is there a specific image that is your favorite or particularly meaningful to this series?

ALF: I am particularly drawn to the landscape imagery in Sown with Salt . What interests me is the tension between the visual experience of the landscape and the complicated environmental history of the places where the images were made.

The project centers on the Mogadore Road brownfield site in Kent, Ohio, the former location of the RB&W industrial fastener plant. The area has a long history of industrial activity and contamination, followed by an ongoing process of remediation. The surrounding landscape can be visually compelling, but that beauty exists alongside a much more complicated history.

That ambiguity is important to me. I don’t want the image to tell the viewer simply that this is a beautiful landscape or that this is a damaged landscape. Both things can be true at the same time. The image becomes a way of entering a larger conversation about memory, environmental change, and the ways we construct meaning around place.

That becomes even more apparent when the imagery enters the book. In Sown with Salt , I use structures such as tunnel books and flag books to layer and repeat images. A tunnel book compresses multiple visual layers into a single sight line, while a flag book creates movement and repetition as it is handled. The image therefore isn’t fixed. It changes depending on how the viewer physically encounters it.

For me, the photograph or print is only one part of the experience. The structure of the book, the paper, the printing process, and the viewer’s physical movement all contribute to the meaning of the image.

©Arron Levi Foster, Du und ich E, Cyanotype on post consumer waste

EK: Can you tell us about your artistic practice?

ALF: I describe my practice as interdisciplinary, research-driven, and site-responsive. I work across printmaking, artists’ books, drawing, photography, video, animation, and installation, but I don’t think of those mediums as isolated from one another. I am interested in what happens when the structures and processes of one medium begin to inform another.

Printmaking and drawing remain foundational because they are deeply connected to process, iteration, and material engagement. I think of print not simply as a means of reproducing an image, but as a way of organizing information, time, and perception.

A major thread running through my work is what I call experiential watchfulness: sustained acts of observing, documenting, researching, and engaging a particular site. I might spend time walking a landscape, making photographs or drawings, studying archival materials, researching its environmental history, and considering how those different forms of knowledge intersect.

That research often leads me toward places where the landscape carries complicated histories, particularly sites affected by industrialization, extraction, migration, environmental degradation, and remediation. I am interested in how those histories remain present even when the physical evidence begins to disappear.

The artist’s book has become particularly important because it gives me a way to make those layers experiential. A book has rhythm and duration. The viewer has to turn a page, unfold a structure, move through a sequence, or physically manipulate the object. Meaning is produced through that interaction.

This connects to my larger interest in the contemporary image environment. We encounter an enormous number of images every day, and most are designed to be consumed almost instantaneously. My work asks what happens when we construct images that resist that speed.

I therefore think of printmaking and book arts as durational image systems. They create conditions for sustained looking, reflection, and physical engagement.

The environmental dimension of the practice has also become increasingly important. I have experimented with reclaimed photographic materials, handmade papers incorporating locally harvested plant matter, botanical dyes, recycled fibers, and other site-responsive materials. For me, material choices are not separate from the conceptual concerns of the work. The ethics and processes of making become part of the research.

©Arron Levi Foster, Sown with salt, Mogadore Rd. (series), Lumen Print, Pigment Print, Handmade Paper, Screenprint

EK: What’s next for you?

ALF: I see the next stage of my practice as an opportunity to push these ideas further. I am particularly interested in continuing to investigate the relationship between artist’s books, expanded print media, photography, and environmental research.

The work has increasingly moved between the individual print, the book, and installation, and I want to continue exploring what happens when those forms overlap. I am also interested in the artist’s book as more than an artwork or container for images. I see it as a research methodology: a structure that can translate landscape into cognitive, temporal, and embodied experience through sequencing, binding, material, and reader interaction.

Having recently relocated to Maine, I am beginning to consider how this research might develop through sustained engagement with the landscapes of Coastal and Southern Maine. I am interested in approaching this new region with the same kind of experiential watchfulness that has shaped my work in Northeast Ohio, spending time with specific sites and allowing the environmental, cultural, and historical complexities of those places to emerge gradually through observation and research.

The shift in geography also opens new questions. Coastal and Southern Maine contain very different relationships between land and water, industry and environment, rural and urban space, tourism and local communities. I am interested in allowing those differences to shape the work rather than simply transferring an existing methodology to a new location.

My curatorial work with Genius Loci: The Pathos of Place , developed with Erik Waterkotte, has expanded this inquiry through collaboration with artists working across different geographic and cultural contexts. The exhibition has reinforced my interest in how artists use print and related media to investigate place, while extending my own studio research into broader professional and scholarly dialogue.

I am also continuing to develop this research through writing and conference presentations. My recent scholarship examines artists’ books as research methodologies, while my upcoming conference work explores print, book arts, and expanded media as forms that unfold through time, physical presence, and embodied engagement.

Having just begun a position as an Assistant Professor of Art and Visual Culture at Bates College, I am excited about the ways teaching, research, and studio practice can inform one another. I want to continue developing my own work while creating opportunities for students to explore artist’s books, independent publishing, alternative photographic processes, and expanded approaches to printmaking.

Ultimately, what is next is a deeper investigation of the same fundamental question that has been present throughout the work: How can an artwork create the conditions for us to slow down, pay attention, and develop a more meaningful relationship to a place?

Epiphany Knedler is an interdisciplinary artist + educator exploring the ways we engage with history. She graduated from the University of South Dakota with a BFA in Studio Art and a BA in Political Science and completed her MFA in Studio Art at East Carolina University. She is based in Aberdeen, South Dakota, serving as an Assistant Professor of Art and Chair of the Art Department at Northern State University, a Content Editor with LENSCRATCH, and the co-founder and curator of the art collective Midwest Nice Art. Her work has been exhibited in the New York Times, the Guardian, Vermont Center for Photography, Lenscratch, Dek Unu Arts, and awarded through Lensculture, the Lucie Foundation, F-Stop Magazine, and Photolucida Critical Mass.

这些景观保持了物理美丽和环境衰退之间的平静紧张,使物理材料和空间序列可以直接参与概念调查的场所。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "几乎,一切构成一个关键项目,在更大的摩加多路系列,扩展这个调查到过程,物质限制,和时间存在。 开发使用交付的摄影纸和简单的皮革摄像机,项目文件网站沿着库亚霍加河盆地。 皮革过程的本质需要延长的存在在每个位置,转化摄影的行为到一个延长的参与与网站。 格式化为一个延长的协议书, 几乎, 所有将这些<unk>形图像转化为一个连续的触摸物体,观众在时间的推移中物理地发展了景观。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在莫加多道系列和几乎,一切,一个图像从来不是一个静态或不中间的记录一个地方;它是一个物质翻译。 通过物理互动,如转页面,转视线,或转动一个序列,观众进入一个空间,在那里时间,过程,触摸变成重要知识方式。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://lenscratch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/©Arron-Foster_Du-und-ich_D.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Lenscratch", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "©Arron Levi Foster, Du und ich D, 消耗废物的基因型", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Epiphany Knedler:你的项目是如何完成的?", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Arron Levi Foster: 这个项目是从我们如何体验和记住地点的更长的研究中发展出来的。 我的背景根源于印刷和绘画,在我的实践中早些时候,我对印刷本质上是基于过程的事实感兴趣。 一个图像是通过层、重复、翻译和积累构成的。 我开始想知道这些品质是否只能用来构建图像,而是结构图像是如何经历的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这个问题最终引导了我超越单独的印刷到序列结构,艺术家的书籍和安装,我越来越感兴趣的是什么会发生,当图像不能立即消耗,而相反,随着时间的推移,页面转动,结构扩展,图像积累,观众必须物理参与工作。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "与此同时,我的研究越来越专注于具体的景观和内在的历史。自2022年以来,我一直在广泛地与超基金和棕色田地在俄亥俄州东北部,包括Kent,Mogadore,Deerfield,Akron和坎顿的地点工作。这些地方由挖掘,工业,环境衰退和修复形成,但它们也是人们生活,记住和构建身份的地方。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "该项目从物质过程、持续观察和环境历史之间的交叉中成长。 更最近,这种思维是通过我的皮<unk>摄影和艺术家的书几乎,一切相结合的。 在我家黑暗室工作时,我获得了大量的过时的摄影纸。 而不是看到这种材料是过时的,我开始思考重复使用、限制和机会作为过程的生产部分。 我用简单的皮<unk>摄像头拍摄沿着库亚霍加河的景点,在那里多样化。曝光要求我留在每个位置一段时间。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这些照片最终成为一个延长的协议书,该项目强化了一个问题,继续塑造我的实践:当一个图像要求我们放缓时会发生什么?", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://lenscratch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/©Arron-Foster_Sown-with-salt_Mogadore-Road_C.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Lenscratch", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "©Arron Levi Foster, 用盐种植, Mogadore Rd. (系列), Lumen 印刷, 色素印刷, 手工制作的纸张, 屏幕印刷", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "问:有没有一个特定的图像是你最喜欢的或 ⁇ 有意义的这个系列?", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "ALF:我特别吸引了Sown with Salt的景观图像,我感兴趣的是景观视觉体验和图像拍摄的地方复杂的环境历史之间的紧张局势。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "该项目中心位于俄亥俄州肯特的莫加德罗路布朗菲尔德站,是RB&W工业固定工厂的前位置,该地区具有工业活动和污染的长期历史,随后正在进行的修复过程,周围的景观可以视觉上令人兴奋,但这种美丽与更复杂的历史相结合。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我不希望图像告诉观众,这只是一个美丽的景观,或者这是一个受损的景观,这两件事都可以同时是真实的,图像成为关于记忆、环境变化以及我们在现场构建意义的更大的谈话的一种方式。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在Sown with Salt中,我使用隧道书和旗帜书等结构来涂层和重复图像,隧道书压缩多个视觉层到一个单一的视线,而旗帜书在处理时创造运动和重复。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对于我来说,摄影或印刷只是体验的一部分,书的结构、纸张、印刷过程以及观众的物理运动都为图像的意义做出贡献。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://lenscratch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/©Arron-Foster_Du-und-ich_E.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Lenscratch", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "©Arron Levi Foster, Du und ich E, 消耗废物的基因型", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "问:你能告诉我们你的艺术实践吗?", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "ALF:我将我的实践描述为跨学科、研究导向和网站响应性,我在印刷、艺术家的书籍、绘画、摄影、视频、动画和安装上工作,但我不认为这些媒体是相互隔离的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "印刷和绘画仍然是基本的,因为它们与处理、 iteration 和物质参与密切相关,我认为印刷不仅仅是重复图像的手段,而且是组织信息、时间和感知的方式。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我的工作中有一大线是我所称之为体验观察:观察、文档、研究和参与一个特定的网站的持续行为,我可能会花时间走路,拍摄照片或绘画,研究档案材料,研究其环境历史,并考虑这些不同知识形式如何相互联系。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种研究往往引导我到景观带有复杂的故事的地方,尤其是由工业化、挖掘、移民、环境衰退和修复所影响的场所,我很感兴趣这些故事在物理证据开始消失时仍然存在。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "艺术家的书已经变得特别重要,因为它给了我一种方式让这些层体验。一本书有节奏和长度.观众必须转页面,开发结构,通过序列移动,或物理操纵对象。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这与我对当代图像环境的兴趣相连,我们每天都会遇到大量的图像,其中大多数图像是为了几乎立即消耗的,我的工作问我们在构建抵抗这种速度的图像时会发生什么。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "因此,我认为印刷和书籍艺术是持久的图像系统,它们创造了持续的视觉、反射和身体参与的条件。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "实践的环境层面也越来越重要,我已经尝试过重新拍摄的照片材料,手工制作的纸质,包含本地收获的植物材料,植物树木,回收的纤维和其他现场响应材料,对我来说,材料选择并不与作品的概念问题分开,制作的道德和过程成为研究的一部分。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://lenscratch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/©Arron-Foster_Sown-With-Salt_Mogadore-Road_B.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Lenscratch", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "©Arron Levi Foster, 用盐种植, Mogadore Rd. (系列), Lumen 印刷, 色素印刷, 手工制作的纸张, 屏幕印刷", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "答:你下一个是什么?", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "ALF:我看到我的实践的下一个阶段是推动这些想法的机会,我特别感兴趣继续研究艺术家的书籍、扩展印刷媒体、摄影和环境研究之间的关系。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "作品越来越多地在个人印刷、书籍和安装之间移动,我想继续探索当这些形状过上时发生的事情,我也对艺术家的书感兴趣,而不是艺术作品或图像容器,我认为它是一种研究方法:可以将景观转化为认知、临时和体现的体验,通过序列、绑定、材料和读者互动。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "最近搬到梅因,我开始考虑如何通过与海岸和南梅因景观的持久参与发展这种研究,我有兴趣以同样的体验性观察性来接近这个新地区,这塑造了我在东北俄亥俄州的工作,花时间与特定地点,并允许这些地点的环境、文化和历史复杂性通过观察和研究逐渐出现。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "地理的转变也开启了新的问题. 海岸和南梅因包含土地和水,工业和环境,农村和城市空间,旅游和当地社区之间的非常不同的关系. 我有兴趣让这些差异塑造工作而不是简单地将现有方法转移到一个新的位置。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "与Erik Waterkotte合作开发的Genius Loci: The Pathos of Place的教科工作,通过与不同地理和文化背景工作的艺术家合作,扩大了这项调查,展览加强了我对艺术家如何使用印刷和相关媒体来调查现场的兴趣,同时将自己的工作室研究扩展到更广泛的专业和学术对话。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我最近的奖学金研究艺术家的书籍作为研究方法,而我的即将到来的会议工作探索印刷,书籍艺术和扩展媒体作为时间,物理存在和体现的参与的形式。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "刚刚开始担任贝茨学院艺术与视觉文化助理教授的职位,我对教学、研究和工作室实践可以互相了解的方式感到兴奋,我想继续发展自己的工作,同时为学生创造机会探索艺术家的书籍、独立出版、替代摄影过程以及扩展的印刷方法。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "最后,接下来是对整个作品中存在的相同基本问题进行更深入的调查:艺术作品如何能为我们创造放缓、注意、发展与某个地方更有意义的关系的条件?", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://lenscratch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/©Arron-Foster_Du-und-ich_F.jpg", excerpt_original: I’ve been acquainted with Arron Levi Foster’s work for a few years now. I first came across it through the exhibition landscapes: peculiar interpretations, exhibited through Midwest Nice Art, an art collective I founded with my husband, Tim Rickett, and has since exhibited with…
translated_title_zh: Arron Levi Foster: 幾乎一切
translated_excerpt_zh: 我已经认识了阿伦·莱维·福斯特(Arron Levi Foster)的作品几年了,我第一次通过展览景观来体验它:通过中西尼西亚艺术展出的独特的解释,我与丈夫蒂姆·里克特(Tim Rickett)一起创立的艺术集合,从那时起就展出了与我相伴的艺术作品。

article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Die Stop-Motion-Filme des Animationsstudios Laika sprengen immer wieder die Grenzen ihrer eigenen Kunstform. Nach 16 Jahren Entstehungszeit startet ihr neustes Werk „Wildwood“ in den Kinos und legt erneut die Messlatte, wie spektakulär handgemachte Animation aussehen kann, ein ganzes Stück höher. Ein Rückblick auf Werke, Geschichte und Philosophie eines Studios, das versucht, einen Funken analoge Magie in unsere digitale Gegenwart zu bringen."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Die Teenagerin Prue radelt durch die Straßen von Portland, Oregon. Es ist ein kalter, klarer Herbsttag, und ihr Fahrrad wirbelt das Laub auf, während ihre Haare im Wind wehen. Nichts an dieser Szene ist real – aber alles ist echt. Prue ist die Protagonistin des Films „ Wildwood “ und wurde vom Animationsstudio Laika zum Leben erweckt. Und dieses Leben findet in Stop-Motion statt. Es gibt ein Modell von Prue, es gibt ihre Kleidung, es gibt Gesichtspartien, die ausgetauscht werden, wenn sie Emotionen zeigt oder spricht. Der Herbstwind existiert nicht, aber das Laub und die wehenden Haare. Und das reicht, um den Wind zu spüren. Schaut man in den Laika-Studios vorbei, die sich ebenfalls in Portland, Oregon, befinden, kann man Prue neben Coraline, Norman und den Boxtrolls in einer Vitrine sehen. Man könnte die Hand ausstrecken und sie anfassen.", "links": [{"text": "Wildwood", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/film/details/627073/wildwood"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/bild/filmdb/378632/wildwood-szenenbild-1.jpg?t=1790777065", "alt": "Laikas jüngste Heldin Prue in „Wildwood“", "caption": "Laikas jüngste Heldin Prue in „Wildwood“ (© Laika/Capelight)", "credit": "Filmdienst"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In einer Zeit, in der CGI-Animation zur Norm geworden ist, hat die aufwändige Stop-Motion-Kunst etwas herrlich Anachronistisches. Man sieht den Unterschied zu Computergrafiken klar und deutlich, sobald man nur darauf achtet: Die Bewegungen sind anders, die Details, die Haptik, das Licht, die Kameraeinstellungen. All das fühlt sich unterschiedlich an. Trotzdem haben die Laika-Filme angesichts ihrer überbordenden Schauwerte ein Luxusproblem: Sie sehen fast zu gut, um wahr zu sein. Logistisch grenzt es an Wahnsinn, derart viel Zeit und Mühe zu investieren, um unzählige Figuren zu erschaffen, sie auf den detailverliebten Sets zu positionieren, um dann 24 Einzelbilder pro Sekunde zu erzeugen. Es ist heutzutage kaum zu glauben, dass solche fulminanten Filmwelten nicht aus einem Computer stammen, sondern das Ergebnis von akribischer Handwerkskunst sind."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Das könnte Sie auch interessieren"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Vom Suchen und Finden des Glücks: Die Filme von DreamWorks Animation", "links": [{"text": "Vom Suchen und Finden des Glücks: Die Filme von DreamWorks Animation", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/artikel/82171/die-animationsfilme-des-dreamworks-studios"}]}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Die Welt mit anderen Augen sehen - Das Pixar-Universum", "links": [{"text": "Die Welt mit anderen Augen sehen - Das Pixar-Universum", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/artikel/61614/die-filme-von-pixar"}]}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Über Nick Park, ,,Aardman Animations‘‘ und die „Wallace & Gromit“-Filme", "links": [{"text": "Über Nick Park, ,,Aardman Animations‘‘ und die „Wallace & Gromit“-Filme", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/artikel/69862/nick-park-wallace-gromit-portrat"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Laika scheint sich dessen bewusst zu sein und wendet einen Kunstgriff an, um die Wahrheit ans Licht zu bringen. Im Abspann jedes Films findet sich ein kurzer Making-of-Clip. Die goldene Regel des Hollywood-Kinos, die Illusion um jeden Preis aufrechtzuhalten, wird geopfert, um zu zeigen, wie viel Arbeit hinter all dem steckt, was sich auf der Leinwand abgespielt hat. Man wird Zeuge, wie Menschen an Modellen basteln, von denen das Kleinste in die Handfläche passt und das größte seine Puppenspieler überragt. In winzigen Schritten mit chirurgischer Präzision werden Gliedmaßen bewegt, Gesichtszüge verändert und Kameras verschoben. Und diese Arbeit ist fast ebenso magisch wie die Abenteuer, die die Figuren in ihren Filmen erleben. Spätestens jetzt, wenn die Erkenntnis einsetzt, dass alles, was man gerade erlebt hat, wirklich auf diese Art entstehen konnte, ist an der Zeit zu staunen."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "The Nightmare Before Laika"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In gewisser Weise beginnt die Geschichte von Laika mit Tim Burton . Allerdings hauptsächlich mit seinem Namen. Eine Dekade, bevor das Animationsstudio gegründet wird, kommt „ Tim Burton's: The Nightmare Before Christmas “ in die Kinos und zeigt, wie erfolgreich Stop-Motion-Filme im sein können. Der Titel ist allerdings ein Werbetrick: Tim Burton ist nicht der Regisseur des Films, sondern lediglich der Autor der Vorlage. Die Umsetzung übernahm Henry Selick . Es ist allerdings kaum verwunderlich, dass Burton mehr Aufmerksamkeit bekommt. Er ist berühmter als Selick und steht genau für die wohlig-gruselige, leicht morbide Stimmung, die der Animationsfilm hervorrufen will. Sogar seine Vita scheint zu passen, denn schon als Kind drehte Burton eigene Stop-Motion-Filme mit der heimischen Kamera und blieb dieser Kunstform später auch in seinen Kurzfilmen treu. In seiner Spielfilmkarriere waren Animationsfilme jedoch die Ausnahme, darum überließ er Selick gerne die Regie. Einige Jahre, nachdem „The Nightmare before Christmas“ zum Hit wurde, nahm ein anderer, prominenter Autor mit Henry Selick Kontakt auf. Neil Gaiman , damals auf einen Karrierehöhepunkt, unterbreitete ihn den Vorschlag, seine fantasievolle Geschichte „Coraline“ zu adaptieren, weil er von „Nightmare Before Christmas“ beeindruckt war. Dieses Treffen fand 2002 statt, drei Jahre bevor Laika überhaupt gegründet wurde.", "links": [{"text": "Tim Burton", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/person/details/1255/tim-burton"}, {"text": "Tim Burton's: The Nightmare Before Christmas", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/film/details/63304/nightmare-before-christmas"}, {"text": "Henry Selick", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/person/details/13332/henry-selick"}, {"text": "Neil Gaiman", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/person/details/207795/neil-gaiman"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Wenn man sich die Filme von Laika ansieht, ist man vielleicht geneigt zu glauben, die Anfänge der Animationsschmiede hätten ähnlich ausgesehen wie die von Tim Burton. Mit Künstler:innen, die mit einer billigen Kamera in ihrer Studenten-WG mühsam kleine Knetfiguren modellieren. Diese romantische Vorstellung ist allerdings weit von der Realität entfernt. Die Erfolgsgeschichte Laikas beginnt wesentlich mondäner: mit einem privilegierten Sohn und einem reichen Vater. Travis Knight wünschte sich, in die Animationsbranche einzusteigen und sein Hobby zum Beruf zu machen. Sein Vater Phil Knight war der Mitgründer von Nike und hatte das Kapital, um seinem Jungen diesen Wunsch zu erfüllen. Er kaufte das kleine Animationsstudio Will Vinton und taufte es 2005 in Laika um – benannt nach dem ersten Hund, der von der Sowjetunion ins Weltall geschossen wurde. Das Studio wurde vergrößert, neue Talente eingestellt, und es gab genügend Geld, um einen ersten Spielfilm zu drehen. Und damit übernahm Travis das Ruder.", "links": [{"text": "Travis Knight", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/person/details/260063/travis-knight"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/bild/filmdb/381736/travis-knight-klein.jpg?t=1793787688", "alt": "Laika-Chef Travis Knight bei der Premiere von „Wildwood“ beim BFI London Filmfestival", "caption": "Laika-Chef Travis Knight bei der Premiere von „Wildwood“ (© imago/Anadolu Agency)", "credit": "Filmdienst"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Bei allem Lobgesang, der hier auf Laika und die dort entstandenen Filme angestimmt wird, soll es vermieden werden, Travis Knight als weißen Ritter im Kreuzzug für die gute Sache zu heroisieren. Er ist wohlhabend genug, um selbst bei größeren Investitionen kein nennenswertes Risiko einzugehen, und selbst seine kommerziell erfolgloseren Filme, sind seiner künstlerischen Karriere zuträglich. Dennoch ist es in einer Zeit, in der viele Milliardäre damit beschäftigt sind, die KI-Apokalypse voranzutreiben oder faschistische Regime zu stärken, erfrischend, wenn zumindest einer seinen Reichtum hauptsächlich nutzt, um mit seinem kreativen Hobby die Welt zu bereichern statt auszubeuten. Zudem zeigt Knight an den richtigen Stellen Bescheidenheit. Zwar ist er federführend im Studio, was die Projektauswahl angeht, aber er drängt sich bei der Umsetzung in den Vordergrund. Gerade zu Beginn seiner Karriere legte er Wert darauf, nicht das letzte Wort bei den Produktionen zu haben, sondern ein Team aus hochtalentierten Kreativen zusammenzustellen. Mit dieser Idee traf er eines Tages Regisseur Henry Selick, der zufälligerweise bereits genau das richtige Projekt im Auge hatte."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "„Coraline“ – Kindheitsalbträume"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Die kleine Coraline scheint perfekt, um in die Fußstapfen von Jack Skellington zu treten. Die schön-schaurige Stimmung ihres Filmes erinnert direkt an „Nightmare Before Christmas“ und sorgt für Gänsehaut in kindgerechtem Ausmaß. Wie Jack ist auch Coraline unzufrieden und gelangweilt von der Welt und entdeckt ein zauberhaftes Paralleluniversum, das all ihren Wünschen zu entsprechen scheint. Doch nach und nach entpuppt sich die alternative Realität, mit ihrer knopfäugigen anderen Mutter, als Albtraum, den sie entkommen muss."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Selick bewährt sich mit „ Coraline “ erneut als Meister seiner Zunft. Der Regisseur übernahm hinter der Kamera einen Teil des Teams, das bereits für „Nightmare before Christmas“ nie dagewesene Stop-Motion-Techniken entwickelt hatte. Bei „Coraline“ fügten die Kreativen ihrem Repertoire noch weitere Tricks hinzu, um ihr neustes Abenteuer bestmöglich zu visualisieren. Der technische Aufwand wird genutzt, um eine fantastische Welt zu erschaffen, die alle paar Minuten mit neuen, erstaunlichen Ideen begeistert.", "links": [{"text": "Coraline", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/film/details/533757/coraline"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/bild/filmdb/314624/coraline-szenenbild-01.jpg?t=1720777626", "alt": "\"Coraline\"", "caption": "\"Coraline\" (© Laika Ent./Universal Pictures)", "credit": "Filmdienst"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Das Debüt der Laika-Studios wurde sofort zum Hit und ist bis heute ein beliebter Kultfilm für die „Spooky Season“ im Oktober. Dieser Erfolg konnte bis heute nicht wiederholt werden: Das kleine, blauhaarige Mädchen lässt alle kommenden Laika-Produktionen an der Kinokasse weit hinter sich zurück. Bis heute hat sie den höchsten Wiedererkennungswert unter allen Figuren des Studios und ist im wahrsten Sinne des Wortes zum Poster-Girl geworden. Noch siebzehn Jahre und vier Spielfilme später steht auf den Filmplakaten von „ Wildwood “: „Von den Machern von ‚Coraline‘“.", "links": [{"text": "Wildwood", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/film/details/627073/wildwood"}]}, {"type": "heading", "text": "„ParaNorman“ – Schrecklich mutig"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Für Laika war „Coraline“ erst der Anfang. Jedes neue Projekt sollte das Studio vor größere, selbstgewählte Herausforderungen stellen. Mit „ ParaNorman “ schufen sie einen weiteren Film, der Halloween-Stimmung verbreitet – sogar noch wesentlich mehr als „Coraline“. „ParaNorman“ spielt in der Kleinstadt Blithe Hollow, deren urbane Legende besagt, dass vor langer Zeit eine böse Hexe hier gelebt habe. Einige Bewohner glauben immer noch, dass sie aus dem Jenseits versucht, die Stadt zu verfluchen. Der junge Norman hat zwar mit dieser Gruselgeschichte nichts zu tun, aber dafür kann er andere Geister sehen. Für ihn sind tote Verwandte, verirrte Seelen und sogar verstorbene Hunde ein ganz normaler Teil des Alltags und jagen ihm keine Angst ein. Um sich zu gruseln, schaut er stattdessen Horrorfilme. Als eines Tages der Fluch der Hexe zur Realität wird und wahrhaftige Zombies aus ihren Gräbern steigen, muss er seine Fähigkeiten nutzen, um die Stadt zu retten.", "links": [{"text": "ParaNorman", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/film/details/540326/paranorman"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/bild/filmdb/381751/paranorman-szenenbild-1.jpg?t=1793795453", "alt": "Gepflegter Grusel: \"ParaNorman\"", "caption": "Gepflegter Grusel: \"ParaNorman\" (© Universal Studios/Laika/Plaion)", "credit": "Filmdienst"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Oberflächlich betrachtet ist „ParaNorman“, genau wie „Coraline“, ein fantasievolles Abenteuer, atmosphärisch verpackt mit einer Vielzahl von familiengerechten Schauermomenten. Doch in diesem Film versteckt sich einer der unglaublichsten Twists der Animationsfilmgeschichte. Die schreckliche Hexe, die im Film die Kleinstadt terrorisiert, ist in Wirklichkeit ein kleines Mädchen namens Agatha. Ungefähr in Normans Alter, das wie er Geister sehen konnte. Doch diese überraschende Wendung allein ist nicht das, was „ParaNorman“ so außergewöhnlich macht. Es sind ihre Umstände: Agatha lebte in einer Zeit, in der diese Gabe sie auf den Scheiterhaufen brachte. Die Zombies, die aus den Gräbern klettern, sind die Stadtältesten, die sie im damaligen Hexenprozess zu Tode verurteilt hatten. In einer Rückblende zum Prozess sieht man die kleine Aggie in einer Ecke kauern und weinen. „ParaNorman“ ist ein Film, in dem eine Gruppe von Erwachsenen ein kleines Mädchen bei lebendigem Leibe auf dem Scheiterhaufen verbrennt. Das muss man erst mal sacken lassen."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alles für diese Entwicklung ist in der Story enorm gut vorbereitet, aber dennoch scheint es quasi unmöglich, von selbst darauf zu kommen, weil dem Publikum im Traum nicht einfallen würde, dass ein Film wie dieser eine derart drastische Richtung einschlägt. Es ist jedoch kein billiger Schockmoment, sondern unterstreicht die Botschaften, die der Film in sich trägt. „ParaNorman“ erzählt von den moralischen Abgründen, die sie auftun, wenn Menschen vor etwas Angst haben und nicht wissen, wie sie damit umgehen sollen. Heutzutage werden keine Hexen mehr verbrannt, aber die Gesellschaft hat andere Wege gefunden, um das Leben von unliebsamen Sonderlingen zu zerstören. Und Norman muss mit seiner Freundesgruppe lernen, wie man mit der Angst der anderen und der eigenen Wut umgehen kann. Zwar gibt es ein versöhnliches Ende, in dem Agatha im Leben nach dem Tod Frieden findet, aber das ändert nichts daran, wie schwer die Themen sind, die hier verhandelt werden, und wie viel Mut dazu gehört, sie in einem familientauglichen Animationsfilm anzusprechen."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Tatsächlich gab es in den USA Gruppen von besorgten Eltern, die zum Boykott des Filmes aufriefen. Jedoch nicht wegen der Grausamkeit gegen Kinder. In der letzten Szene des Filmes findet Normans Schwester endlich den Mut, ihren Schwarm auf einen Filmabend einzuladen. Der etwas naive Football-Spieler versteht nicht, dass es sich dabei um ein Date handelt, und würde gerne seinen „Boyfriend“ mitbringen. Die bloße Existenz von Homosexualität hatte in konservativen Kreisen offensichtlich mehr Sorgen hervorgerufen als Kindermord."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Auf die Frage, warum Laika trotz aller Widerstände diese künstlerischen Entscheidungen getroffen hat, gibt Regisseur Chris Butler die perfekte Antwort: „Wenn wir den Zuschauern unseres Films vermitteln möchten, dass sie andere nicht verurteilen sollen, müssen wir auch die Stärke haben, zu diesen Überzeugungen zu stehen.“", "links": [{"text": "Chris Butler", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/person/details/260061/chris-butler"}]}, {"type": "heading", "text": "„Boxtrolls“ – Die Außenseiterbanden"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Die Geschichten der Laika-Filme stellen häufig Außenseiter in den Mittelpunkt. Sei es die fantasievolle Coraline, die von ihren Eltern nicht ernst genommen wird, oder Normans Bande von missverstandenen Jugendlichen. Alle fallen gerade genug aus dem gesellschaftlichen Rahmen, dass es ihnen schwerfällt, in der normalen, langweiligen Welt Kontakte zu knüpfen. Am deutlichsten ausgespielt wird dieser Topos bei „ Boxtrolls “, in dem sich eine komplette Parallelgesellschaft gebildet hat, die versteckt im Untergrund leben muss, um das Spießbürgertum nicht zu erschrecken.", "links": [{"text": "Boxtrolls", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/film/details/544615/die-boxtrolls"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Die Boxtrolls wohnen im schrulligen Cheesebridge, in dem die Leute ein behütetes Leben führen und einflussreiche Männer in einer elitären Gesellschaft Käse verkosten. Als eines Tages ein Kind verschwindet, wird schnell den Trollen die Schuld gegeben. Es beginnt eine gnadenlose Jagd auf die friedlichen Kreaturen, die einfach nur Spaß daran haben, durch den Müll zu wühlen und aus ihren Fundstücken kleine Gerätschaften zu basteln. Das Baby, das bei den Trollen landet, wird in einen Eierkarton gesteckt, erhält den Namen „Eggs“ und muss den zutraulichen Kreaturen dabei helfen, die Wahrheit ans Licht zu bringen."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/bild/filmdb/203057/die-boxtrolls-szenenbild-2.jpg?t=1588672299", "alt": "Charmante Sonderlinge: \"Die Boxtrolls\" ", "caption": "Charmante Sonderlinge: \"Die Boxtrolls\" (© Universal Pictures International Germany GmbH)", "credit": "Filmdienst"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Die Dynamik, die zwischen Trollen und Menschen herrscht, ist der in „ParaNorman“ nicht unähnlich: Beide Gruppen haben Angst voreinander, und bei einer davon schlägt dies in Wut um. Ehe man sich‘s versieht, wird aus einem kulturellen Missverständnis eine Geschichte von Tätern und Opfern. Die Lösung, einander zuzuhören und voneinander zu lernen, ist wie immer naheliegend, aber in den starren gesellschaftlichen Konventionen leichter gesagt als getan."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Obwohl „Boxtrolls“ in einem imaginären europäischen Land spielen, durchweht ihn eine gewisse Britishness. Ben Kingsley synchronisiert den Schurken, während Eric Idle das Lied für den Abspann zum Besten gibt. Die Stadt, mit ihren verwinkelten Gässchen, in denen die Schornsteine rauchen und alte Herrenclubs den Ton angeben, erinnert an die Zeiten der englischen Industrialisierung. Und möglicherweise ist die eigenartige Vorliebe für Käse sogar eine Hommage – oder gar ein Seitenhieb – auf das prominenteste Stop-Motion-Duo des Vereinigten Königreichs: „Wallace & Gromit“."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "„Kubo – Der tapfere Samurai“ & die Kunst des Erzählens"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In „ Kubo – Der tapfere Samurai “ entführt Laika das Publikum dagegen in die Welt der asiatischen Mythologie. Allerdings nicht auf eine völlig unproblematische Art und Weise. Trotz des erklärten Willens zur Toleranz und Repräsentation ist fast das komplette Synchron-Ensemble mit weißen Stars besetzt. Charlize Theron, Matthew McConaughey und Ralph Fiennes leihen ihre Stimmen Figuren, die durch das Setting eindeutig japanisch angelegt sind. Zumindest George Takei hat eine kleine Gastrolle bekommen. Abgesehen davon ist die Art und Weise, wie die abgebildete Kultur dargestellt wird, ihren Wurzeln unheimlich treu. Enorm viel Recherche und Beratung floss in eine Welt, die sich vor den Mythologien und Einflüssen, die sie darstellt, tief verbeugt. Travis Knight , der bei „Kubo“ zum ersten Mal in der Studiogeschichte selbst die Regie übernahm, hat offensichtlich Respekt vor seinen Inspirationsquellen – nur leider nicht so viel, um es seine Castingentscheidungen beeinflussen zu lassen. Möglicherweise wollte er bei seinem Debüt sichergehen, dass der Film genügend Werbewirkung entfaltet.", "links": [{"text": "Kubo – Der tapfere Samurai", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/film/details/548546/kubo-der-tapfere-samurai"}, {"text": "Travis Knight", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/person/details/260063/travis-knight"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Abseits von dieser Kontroverse über kulturelle Aneignung, ist „Kubo“ ein beeindruckendes Werk. Es ist ein Miniaturfilm von gigantischem Ausmaß. Laike baute enorme Sets, um die großangelegten Kampfszenen richtig in Szene zu setzen. Wenn der kleine Samurai gegen riesige Skelette und monströse Unterwasserkreaturen in Feld zieht, wurde nicht in der Kamera getrickst, sondern alle Modelle wurden im realen Maßstab gebaut. Es entsteht ein atemberaubendes Spektakel mit Material-Arts-Kämpfen, in denen ein schwertschwingender Affe gegen eine fliegende Hexe auf einem sinkenden Schiff im Regen kämpft. Und all das ist genauso spektakulär, wie es sich anhört."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/bild/filmdb/381738/kubo-der-tapfere-samurai-szenenbild-1.jpg?t=1793795208", "alt": "Fantastische Abenteuer: \"Kubo - Der tapfere Samurai\"", "caption": "Fantastische Abenteuer: \"Kubo - Der tapfere Samurai\" (© Laika/Plaion)", "credit": "Filmdienst"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Wie viele Laika-Protagonisten wird auch Kubo in eine Zauberwelt gezogen, die es jenseits der bekannten Realität zu erforschen gilt. Doch die Geschichte des kleinen Samurais beginnt erstaunlich langsam. Bevor er ins Abenteuer aufbricht und mit sprechenden Affen und kriegerischen Käfern gegen Dämonen kämpft, muss er sich zunächst um seine kranke Mutter kümmern. Der Prolog beginnt zwar temporeich, voller Gefahren und wogender Wellen, aber er widmet sich nach seinem pompösen Auftakt in respektvoller Ruhe der Familienbeziehung. Der Angst einer Mutter, sich nicht mehr um ihren Sohn kümmern zu können, und der Angst eines Sohnes, seine Mutter zu verlieren. Dieses Mal wird daraus keine Wut. Sondern Trauer."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Die Action in „Kubo“ ist zwar restlos beeindruckend, doch das Herz der Erzählung ist in ihren ruhigen Momenten zu finden. Knight mischt östliche und westliche Philosophie, um daraus einen Film über Verlust und Trauerarbeit zu machen. Die Einsicht, die er Kubo dabei mit auf den Weg gibt, könnte auch die Kernphilosophie der Laika-Studios sein: Wir können nicht alles Unheil der Welt aufhalten – aber wir können Geschichten erzählen, die es leichter zu ertragen machen."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "„Mister Link“ – Gemeinsam gegen das Establishment"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Laikas folgender Film, „Mister Link – Ein fellig verrücktes Abenteuer“ verabschiedet sich von dieser Gedankenschwere und spielt mit Mustern einer klassischen Buddy-Comedy: Der arrogante Lionel, ein britischer Gentleman-Abenteurer des 19. Jahrhunderts, ist auf der Jagd nach unentdeckten Kreaturen. Er findet einen naiven Sasquatch, den er „Mister Link“ tauft. Link, der sich später den Namen Susan gibt, sucht nach seiner Familie, und Lionel sucht nach Ruhm. So müssen die beiden ungleichen Gefährten zu Freunden werden, um auf einer chaotischen Reise durch die tiefsten Dschungel und auf die höchsten Gipfel zu bestehen. Trotz beeindruckender Schauplätze und wunderschön animierter Naturwunder sprengt Laika zum ersten Mal nicht die Dimensionen ihres vorigen Films. „Mister Link“ ist eine kleinere Geschichte, ohne große Philosophie, aber mit jeder Menge humorvollen Verstrickungen an exotischen Orten."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/bild/filmdb/162935/mister-link-7.jpg?t=1556801259", "alt": "Ziemlich beste Freunde: Die Helden von \"Mister Link\"", "caption": "Ziemlich beste Freunde: Die Helden von \"Mister Link\" (© eOne)", "credit": "Filmdienst"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Thematisch findet sich allerdings ein interessantes Echo in „Mister Link“ wieder. Obwohl die wackeren Abenteurer zu einer weltumspannenden Reise aufbrechen, beginnen sie an einem vertrauten Ort: in einem Gentleman-Club. Dieses Mal wirklich in England. Lionel möchte unbedingt der „Society of Great Men“ beitreten, die sich wie ein Gegenstück zu dem elitären Käseclub in „Boxtrolls“ anfühlt. Im Laufe der Reise stellt sich heraus, dass Susan ein ähnliches Ziel verfolgt. Beide würden gerne ihre Einzigartigkeit opfern, um Teil einer prestigeträchtigen Gruppe zu werden. Und beide müssen lernen, dass das, was sie suchen, nicht unbedingt das ist, was sie brauchen. Die selbsternannten „Great Men“ glänzen, wie ihre Äquivalente in anderen Laika-Filmen, durch grenzenlosen Egoismus. Ihr größter Wunsch ist es, unter sich zu bleiben und weder ihre Macht noch ihr Geld dazu einzusetzen, die Welt auch nur einen Hauch zum Besseren zu verändern. Vielleicht dient dieses wiederkehrende Muster Travis Knight als Erinnerung, trotz seines privilegierten Lebens, nie selbst einer von diesen Great Men zu werden, sondern einer von den Sonderlingen zu bleiben."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "„Wildwood“ – Tiefer in die Wälder"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Mit seinem neuesten Film „ Wildwood “ zementiert das Studio nach siebenjähriger Pause seinen Ruf als eine der kreativsten Animationsschmieden der Gegenwart.
